title: Sikh soldiers under the Raj
hookLine: after the great rising against Company rule, the British recruited Sikhs heavily into the army

cards: A barracks at dawn, a very long way from Punjab: a hot port, a cold frontier, a city where nobody speaks Punjabi. Rows of young men tie their turbans before parade.
In one room, set apart, a granthi opens the Guru Granth Sahib and reads the morning's hymn. These soldiers wear the uniform of the British Crown.
Not long before, men from the same villages had fought the British at Ferozeshah and Sobraon.

teach.b: After the wars and the annexation, the British army in India was shaken by a great rising against Company rule. Punjab did not join it in strength, and Sikh soldiers fought on the British side.

After that, the British looked to Punjab for soldiers, and Sikhs were recruited heavily. British officers came to call Sikhs a martial race, a label about whole peoples that historians now treat with care.

teach.h: THE ARMY WANTED THE KHALSA FORM.
teach.b: And the army wanted its Sikh soldiers to look like Khalsa Sikhs: uncut hair, the turban, the outward form. Some histories argue that this helped keep the Khalsa form strong in villages at a time when it might have faded.

teach.h: THE GURU WENT WITH THE REGIMENT.
teach.b: Sikh regiments carried the Guru Granth Sahib with them, with a granthi to read it, so a soldier posted far from home could still hear the hymns in the morning.
Service took these men to garrisons and battlefields across the empire, far from wives, parents and fields.
In a hymn of Guru Ram Das in Raag Asa, the Guru says that wherever the true Guru goes and sits, that place is made beautiful.
A barracks room far from Punjab, with the Guru Granth Sahib open in it, could be read that way.
But the uniform belonged to a foreign Crown, and Sikhs still talk about what that meant: honor, a living for poor families, and a hard question about whose battles they were fighting.

how: Sikh regiments have kept the Guru Granth Sahib with them, read by a regimental granthi, and Sikh families remember soldier ancestors who served overseas in the British Indian Army.

games.q: you're a young Sikh in a Punjab village after the kingdom has fallen. a recruiter offers pay and a uniform. which way did the story of these years go, as the histories tell it?

games.why: Sikhs were recruited heavily, and served in garrisons across the empire, keeping the turban and the Guru's hymns in the barracks.

practice: Picture a soldier far from home, from any country and any time, in the first quiet minutes of the day: a turban tied the way it was tied at home, a photo tucked in a pocket, a few lines of a hymn or a letter read again.
Notice how small the things are that they carry, ask what small thing you carry into the hard places of your own day, and wish that soldier home safely. If you pray, add Waheguru to the wish.
